1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying, Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord God; Howl ye, Woe worth the day! For the day is near, even the day of the Lord is near, a cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen. And the sword shall come upon Egypt, and great pain shall be in Ethiopia, when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down. Ethiopia, and Libya, and Lydia, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. Thus saith the Lord; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down: from the tower of Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord God. And they shall be desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate, and her cities shall be in the midst of the cities that are wasted. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have set a fire in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be destroyed. In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Ethiopians afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh. Thus saith the Lord God; I will also make the multitude of Egypt to cease by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the terrible of the nations, shall be brought to destroy the land: and they shall draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain. And I will make the rivers dry, and sell the land into the hand of the wicked: and I will make the land waste, and all that is therein, by the hand of strangers: I the Lord have spoken it. Thus saith the Lord God; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt. And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No. And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No. And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily. The young men of Aven and of Pi–beseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity. At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity. Thus will I execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I am the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch say the heading gives no chronological information and the contents no criteria, note that one ancient authority put this oracle with the first Egyptian one while several moderns make it the latest thing in the book, and set out its shape instead: a call to lamentation, then three sections marked by one formula, the destruction of Egypt's might, the enemy who executes judgment, and the extermination of the idols. Ellicott lifts the passage out of Egyptian history, since the judgment here is one instance and a symbol of the judgment on every merely worldly power, this fall being a single step in the general overthrow of whatever exalts itself against God, which is why so many other prophets use the same language; he calls the English equivalents of the allied peoples an unfortunate substitution for the original terms kept elsewhere in the book, and adds that both supplied mercenaries to Tyre and more to Egypt; he rules the Babylonians out as the messengers in ships on historical grounds, that army never having penetrated so far, and makes them fleeing Egyptians who go up the river for safety and alarm the country, the careless being the Ethiopians in their security and the day of Egypt a past judgment at the exodus; he works through the city names, the capital of Lower Egypt near the pyramids, the celebrated city of Upper Egypt whose ruins still stand, the frontier fortress rightly called the key of Egypt and here called its strength, and the city named from a cat-headed goddess, noting that the vowels of one name were altered to make it read as nothingness, a word often used of idols; and he takes the promise about a prince relatively, that there shall be no native prince holding the old kings' power.

Gill weighs whether the oracle belongs with the earlier or later part of the preceding chapter and inclines to the later, since the fulfilment is said to be near; he traces the allied peoples to the sons and grandsons of Ham and thinks the usual English equivalents proper enough; on the messengers in ships he offers three possibilities, Babylonian vessels, men moved by providence to carry the news, and the king himself coming with his army; and with Clarke he derives the frontier city's name from a word for clay.

Clarke gives the chapter's architecture and observes that the closing verses, a separate and earlier prophecy, were annexed because they concern the same event; he stops over the opening cry to give an old manuscript Bible's rendering in its own spelling and note that the current wording came from a printed Bible of 1536; he suspects a corruption in one of the allied names and would read all the men of the land, the Greek version adding two peoples not in the Hebrew; he makes the messengers in ships Babylonian, vessels being able to ascend past the cataracts and Nebuchadnezzar's boats having struck terror into the Ethiopians; and he takes the promise about a prince absolutely, saying there has been none from that day to his own. Wesley says times of trouble are called cloudy days, distinguishes the African people from the Asiatic kingdom of the same English name and places them between Cyrene and Egypt, guesses another name may cover the Nubians of his day, takes the mingled people for hired soldiers, agrees the messengers are survivors of the sword carrying the report, and offers both senses of the promise about a prince without choosing.

Henry hears the summons as a taunt turned inside out: howl now that it is coming, since you will be made to howl when it comes; you have your day now, carrying all before you and trampling those about you, but God will have his shortly. The cloudy day he takes for one dark and dismal, threatening a storm.

debates.question: Who are the messengers who go forth in ships?

positions.position: Babylonian, since vessels can ascend past the cataracts and Nebuchadnezzar's boats terrified the Ethiopians.
Fleeing Egyptians going upriver for safety; the Babylonian army never penetrated so far.
Any of three: Babylonian vessels, men moved by providence, or the king with his army.

debates.question: How absolute is the promise that Egypt shall have no prince?

positions.position: Absolute; there has been none from that day to the present.
Relative; no native prince holding the power of the former kings.
Either an Egyptian by birth or an independent ruler over the whole country; both senses are offered.

outliers.claim: Quotes an old English manuscript Bible's rendering of the opening cry in its own spelling, and notes that the wording of the received version was taken over from a printed Bible of 1536.
Calls the familiar English names of two allied peoples an unfortunate substitution for the original terms, which the same book preserves correctly elsewhere.

20.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day of the month, that the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword. Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken; and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword in his hand: but I will break Pharaoh’s arms, and he shall groan before him with the groanings of a deadly wounded man. But I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh shall fall down; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them among the countries; and they shall know that I am the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the clause about the broken arm as applying remedies and binding the limb so it might grow strong enough to grasp a sword again. Ellicott dates the oracle a little more than three months and a half before the fall of the city and thinks it occasioned by the temporary lifting of the siege when the Egyptian king came up and was driven off, news which would have taken months to reach Chaldea; he takes the perfect tense of the broken arm to point back to earlier conquests and above all to the great battle some twenty years before, from which Egypt never recovered; and he modernises one word, since what the older version calls a roller would now be called a bandage.

Gill says that with this verse the prophecies come back into their sequence after being interrupted by pieces of much later date; he rejects the reading that refers the broken arm to the earlier Pharaoh, naming two Jewish commentators who hold it, and refers it instead to the reigning king, defeated by the Cyreneans and saved only by flight; and he places the scattered exiles among the provinces of Babylon.

Clarke draws a conclusion about the book from the date, since this is an earlier prophecy than the long one just given, so whoever collected these writings took more care to put everything on one subject together than to keep chronological order; he offers a third and more recent occasion for the broken arm, the repulse of the Egyptian army that had come up to relieve Jerusalem; he keeps to the mechanics, that a broken arm drops its weapon, and takes the language to mean Egypt would be of no further use to the king of Judah and would never recover its political strength, which he dates from a later rebellion; and he reports that some fled with their king into Upper Egypt while Nebuchadnezzar carried many away when he wasted the country. Wesley gives the interval as three months and two days and assigns the same occasion as Ellicott, takes in both the Chaldean victory over the one king and the Cyrenean victory over the other without choosing, and draws from the strengthening of Babylon's arms that a judge on the bench and a general in the field are alike, neither having any power except what is given from above.

Henry frames the oracle as two states passing each other, since Egypt was ancient and long considerable while Babylon had only lately come to its pomp, built on the ruins of Assyria, and it is with kingdoms as with families, some growing and others going back, so one must increase while the others decrease. He turns the refusal of treatment into a rule, that God's judgments come by steps so that men may meet him repenting, and that when he breaks an arm it is not bound up, since none can heal the wounds God gives but himself and those he disarms cannot hold the sword again. On the second stroke he reads the ordinary method of judgment, that where lesser corrections fail greater ones follow, observes that the sword falls from a hand that had gripped it thinking itself strong enough, holds that power abused either to wrong people or to cheat them is justly broken, and notes the king groans as a man mortally wounded before the sword has touched him, since those most elated in prosperity are commonly the most dejected in adversity.

debates.question: Which defeat is the arm already broken?

positions.position: The great battle some twenty years earlier, from which Egypt never recovered.
Not that battle but the reigning king's defeat by the Cyreneans, from which he escaped by flight.
Perhaps the recent repulse of the Egyptian army that came up to relieve Jerusalem.
Both the Chaldean victory over the one king and the Cyrenean victory over the other.

debates.question: Why does this dated oracle stand after an undated one that is later?

positions.position: Because the collector grouped the writings by subject rather than by date.
Because with this verse the prophecies resume their proper sequence after an interruption by later pieces.

outliers.claim: Reads the two kingdoms as a single accounting, since one must increase exactly as the other decreases, Babylon having been built on the ruins of Assyria while Egypt had been considerable for ages.
Modernises the surgical vocabulary, observing that the roller of the older version would now simply be called a bandage.
